subtopics.title: Composition and Necessity of the Public Sector

questions.question: The three tiers of government in South Africa, with an example function each, are:
options: National (policy and departments such as police), provincial (schools and hospitals), local (water, refuse and municipal roads)
Parliament, the courts and the Reserve Bank
Eskom, Transnet and the SABC
The IMF, the World Bank and the WTO

questions.question: A PUBLIC good is defined by being:
options: Free of charge and produced by any firm
Non-rivalrous (one person's use leaves no less for another) and non-excludable (non-payers cannot be fenced out)
Rivalrous and excludable
Any good sold by a state-owned enterprise

questions.question: The FREE-RIDER problem means that:
options: Taxi fares are subsidised
Government employees travel without paying
Since non-payers cannot be excluded from a public good, everyone waits for others to pay and no private firm can supply it
Imports enter the country without duties

questions.question: Basic education and vaccination are called MERIT goods because:
options: Only the wealthy consume them
They are awarded for good performance
They earn export revenue
Their benefits spill over to society, so the market left alone provides too little of them

subtopics.title: Problems of Provisioning and the Objectives of the Public Sector

questions.question: Accountability is a provisioning problem because:
options: The link between paying and receiving is cut — officials spend money that is not theirs and voters discipline them only every five years
Taxes are too low to fund services
Auditors-general are unconstitutional
Customers can easily switch to another government

questions.question: Assessing needs is hard for the state because:
options: Citizens have no needs
Unlike a market reading demand off prices, the state must estimate need through surveys, censuses and politics — and the loudest voice is not always the greatest need
Surveys are illegal
Prices always reveal need perfectly to government

questions.question: The parastatal problem, with Eskom as the standing example, is that state-owned enterprises:
options: Are always profitable
Face too much competition
Must run commercially while also serving social goals, and the tension shows in debt and failing delivery
Are owned by foreign shareholders

questions.question: The five macroeconomic objectives of the public sector are:
options: Privatisation, nationalisation, taxation, borrowing, spending
Higher tariffs, lower wages, more exports, less saving, stable gold prices
Free water, free electricity, free transport, free housing, free data
Economic growth, full employment, price stability, exchange-rate stability and economic equity

subtopics.title: The Budget, Fiscal Policy and the Laffer Curve

questions.question: Direct and indirect taxes are, respectively:
options: Taxes on income such as personal and company tax; taxes on spending such as VAT and excise duties
Taxes paid in cash; taxes paid electronically
National taxes; municipal taxes
VAT; personal income tax

questions.question: VAT is described as regressive in effect because:
options: Its rate rises with income
The poor spend a larger share of their income, so a flat rate on spending takes a larger share of a poor household's income
Only companies pay it
It is zero-rated on luxury goods

questions.question: A budget DEFICIT is:
options: Revenue exceeding spending
Revenue equal to spending
Spending exceeding revenue, financed by issuing government bonds that accumulate as public debt
The total of all taxes collected

questions.question: On the Laffer curve, tax revenue is zero at BOTH a zero rate and a hundred percent rate because:
options: The curve is drawn incorrectly
Government refuses to collect at those rates
Revenue is always zero whatever the rate
At zero nothing is levied, and at a hundred percent no one works or declares income to be taxed away entirely

questions.question: Public sector failure occurs when:
options: Government intervention allocates resources LESS efficiently than the market it meant to improve on
Any tax is collected
The market provides public goods
A budget surplus is recorded

questions.question: Which list contains CAUSES of public sector failure?
options: Externalities, public goods and merit goods
Management failure, apathy, bureaucracy, politics overriding economics, and corruption
Growth, employment and price stability
Non-rivalry and non-excludability

questions.question: Public sector failure hurts the poor most because:
options: The poor pay the most company tax
Grants are only paid to the wealthy
The wealthy buy private substitutes for failing schools, health and security, while the poor cannot
The poor do not use public services

questions.question: The balanced conclusion the essay requires is:
options: The state should replace all markets
Markets never fail
Neither failure can be corrected
Market failure justifies a public sector and public sector failure disciplines it — the question is which failure is worse in the case at hand, and how each is corrected

subtopics.title: What the Street Cannot Buy for Itself

questions.question: The bread and the taxi ride are private goods because:
options: The seller can exclude non-payers — you pay, you get
They are subsidised by government
Everyone consumes them equally
They are non-rivalrous

questions.question: The streetlight stays dark without government because:
options: Electricity cannot reach the street
Each neighbour waits for the others to pay, since no one can be excluded from the light once it burns
Streetlights are illegal to buy privately
The municipality forbids it

questions.question: The clinic sits between the bread and the streetlight because:
options: It is non-rivalrous like the streetlight
It cannot charge fees at all
It could charge fees, but vaccination and education carry benefits that spill past the buyer, so the market alone would buy too little
Its services are demerit goods

questions.question: The social grant corrects the market's income distribution because:
options: It is a payment for labour supplied
It is a loan that must be repaid
It is a tax on spending
The market pays what labour fetches, not what a family needs — redistribution answers need

subtopics.title: Why the Tap Runs Slow — the Trouble with Providing

questions.question: The bakery stays sharp and the licensing office often does not because:
options: The bakery faces a daily vote — bad bread empties the till tomorrow — while the office's customers cannot go elsewhere and its funding arrives regardless
Bakers are more honest people
The office has fewer customers
Bread is a public good

questions.question: The stepped water tariff — first kilolitres free, then rising blocks — answers the pricing puzzle by:
options: Charging everyone full cost
Making basic need free while charging luxury use dearly, so the poor can cook and the reservoir is not emptied on driveways
Making all water free
Privatising the water system

questions.question: The department cannot bake like the bakery because:
options: It has too much money
Its ovens are older
No price tells it how many houses or nurses are needed — it must guess through surveys, censuses and politics
Demand for houses does not exist

questions.question: "Serve the social goal and the balance sheet bleeds; serve the balance sheet and the villages go dark" describes:
options: The free-rider problem
The Laffer curve
Progressive taxation
The parastatal tension — a state enterprise pulled between commercial survival and social mandates

subtopics.title: February's Envelope and the Tax That Bites Back

questions.question: The main money INTO February's envelope comes from:
options: Income tax on workers, VAT from every till slip, company tax, and duties on fuel, alcohol and tobacco
Selling gold reserves
Printing new banknotes
Donations from other countries

questions.question: Borrowing every year just to pay salaries and interest is dangerous because:
options: Borrowing is always wrong
This year's classroom is funded by next year's taxpayer, and interest becomes one of the fastest-growing items in the budget
It strengthens the rand too much
Ports can never be built with loans

questions.question: In the spaza-tax story, pushing the rate past the crest of the hump means:
options: Revenue rises without limit
The shop pays double tax happily
Each extra percent collects LESS, as people work less, hide sales or slip into the informal economy
The government must lower VAT

questions.question: The evaluation mark on the Laffer curve is earned by adding that:
options: The curve proves taxes should be zero
The curve only applies to VAT
Revenue is highest at a hundred percent
Nobody knows precisely where the crest sits — the curve argues for caution, not a precise instruction
